title: Consider the lilies
hookLine: Solomon in all his glory wasn't dressed like one of these (Matthew 6:28–29)

cards: Most feet step right over it: a weed growing out of a crack in the sidewalk, with one yellow flower. Nobody planted it. Nobody waters it.

Everyone's on the way to somewhere important. In the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew's Gospel has Jesus point his listeners at exactly this kind of thing: not a temple, not a sunset, but wildflowers in a field.
And he sets them beside a king: Solomon, in all his glory. The flowers, he says, win.

teach.b: First, the instruction. In the King James words: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin". Consider is the verb.
Not glance at, not admire in passing: look long enough to see how they grow.
Second, the comparison: "And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." All that wealth, all that work, and a flower that did nothing outdressed it.
Awe here doesn't come from size. It comes from looking closely at something ordinary until it stops being ordinary. Third, the setting.
The lilies sit inside a passage about worry. Just before them come the birds: "they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them."
Just after, the grass of the field, "which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven". The flowers don't last.
That's part of the point: something that won't be here next week is still dressed with care today.
Fourth, where it lands: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." In the passage, take no thought is about worry, not about planning.
For Christians, the lilies point to God's care. For anyone, they offer a small door out of tomorrow's list and into this one living thing, right now.

how: Christians read this passage from the Sermon on the Mount as a teaching on trust in God's care; some people on other paths use it as a prompt to spend a few minutes studying one plant or flower closely.

games.q: Jesus wants to show how well the lilies are dressed. who does he compare them to?
o: the high priest in his robes.
games.why: Solomon in all his glory, and the wildflower still wins.

practice: Find one flower, a houseplant, a weed, a bouquet, or a leaf or a photo if that's what's near, and look at it as if you had to describe it to someone who's never seen one: the color at the center, the shape of each petal, where the stem bends.
When your mind slips to tomorrow's list, come back to the flower. If you pray, the looking can become thanks.

wordCard.voice: Solomon. The king in all his glory, whom Jesus said was not arrayed like a single wildflower that does no work. Today's word.
